drachma.e: Borrowed from Latin drachma and its etymon Doric Greek δρᾰχμᾱ́ (drăkhmā́).
drachma.g: The currency of Greece in ancient times and again from 1832 until 2001, with the symbol ₯, since replaced by the euro.

drag.e: From Middle English draggen (“to drag”), early Middle English dragen (“to draw, carry”), confluence of Old English dragan (“to drag, draw, draw oneself, go, protract”) and Old Norse draga (“to draw, attract”); both from Proto-Germanic *draganą (“to draw, drag”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰregʰ- (“to draw, drag”).
drag.g: Resistance of a fluid to something moving through it.

drag.e: Possibly from English drag (“to pull along a surface”) because of the sensation of long skirts trailing on the floor, or from Yiddish טראָגן (trogn, “to wear”)
drag.g: A performance art form associated with the LGBTQ+ community, that features a stylized and exaggerated portrayal of femininity or, at times,

dragnet.e: From drag + net, probably based on the model of Middle English draynet, dreynett (“dragnet”), Old English dræġnet, dræġnett (“dragnet”), equivalent to dray + net.
dragnet.g: A net dragged across the bottom of a body of water.

dragon.e: From Middle English dragoun, borrowed from Old French dragon, from Latin dracō(n), from Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, “a serpent of huge size, a python, a dragon”), probably from δέρκομαι (dérkomai, “to see clearly”). Mostly displaced Old English draca (whence modern drake)—from the same Latin source, as are Draco, Dracon, dracone, and dragoon.
dragon.g: A mythical reptilian or serpentine creature.
dragon.sf: From Ancient Greek δράκων (drákōn, “a serpent of huge size, a python, a dragon”)

drain.e: From Middle English *dreinen, from Old English drēahnian, from Proto-West Germanic *drauhnōn, from Proto-Germanic *drauhnōną, from *draugiz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrewgʰ-, from *dʰer-.
drain.g: A conduit allowing liquid to flow out of an otherwise contained volume; a plughole (UK)

dram.e: From Middle English dragme /dramme, from Old French dragme, from Late Latin dragma, from Latin drachma, from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ, “unit of weight; a handful”).
dram.g: A small unit of weight, variously:

dram.e: Borrowed from Armenian դրամ (dram), from Middle Persian 𐭦𐭥𐭦𐭭 (ZWZN /⁠drahm⁠/), from Ancient Greek δραχμή (drakhmḗ, “unit of weight, a handful”), from δράσσομαι (drássomai, “to hold, seize”).
dram.g: The currency of Armenia, divided into 100 luma.

drank.e: From Middle English drank, from Old English dranc, from Proto-West Germanic *drank.

drape.e: From Middle English drape (“a drape”, noun), from Old French draper (“to drape; to full cloth”), from drap (“cloth, drabcloth”).

draught.e: From Middle English draught, draght, draȝt, from Old English *dreaht, *dræht (related to dragan (“to draw, drag”)), from Proto-Germanic *drahtuz, noun form of *draganą; equivalent to draw + -t.
draught.g: Alternative form of draft in some of its senses.

drawer.e: From draw (“to move by pulling”) + -er; compare French tiroir.

drawers.e: From draw (“to pull”), hence that which is pulled onto the body.
drawers.g: Clothing worn on the legs, especially that worn next to the skin, such as hose or breeches.

drawing.e: From Middle English drauinge, drawinge, alteration of earlier drawende, drawand, from Old English dragende, from Proto-Germanic *dragandz (“drawing”), present participle of Proto-Germanic *draganą (“to draw; pull”), equivalent to draw + -ing.

dread.e: From Middle English dreden, from Old English drǣdan (“to fear, dread”), aphetic form of ondrǣdan (“to fear, dread”), from Proto-West Germanic *andarādan, equivalent to Old English and- + rǣdan (whence read); corresponding to an aphesis of earlier adread.
From Middle English drede, dred, from the verb (see above).
dread.g: Great fear in view of impending evil; fearful apprehension of danger; anticipatory terror.

dreadful.e: From Middle English dredful, dredfull, dredeful (also dreful). By surface analysis, dread + -ful.
dreadful.g: Full of something causing dread, whether

dreads.e: Abbreviation of dreadlocks. Sense of “Rastafarian person” by synecdoche.

dream.e: From Middle English dream, dreem, dreeme, drem, dreme, dræm, from Old English drēam, drēm, drīm (“joy; melody, music; frenzy”), from Proto-West Germanic *draum, from Proto-Germanic *draumaz (“dream”), from earlier *draugmaz, from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrowgʰ-mos, from *dʰrewgʰ- (“to deceive”).
dream.g: Imaginary events seen in the mind while sleeping.

dreamer.e: From Middle English dremer, dremere, dremare, equivalent to dream + -er.

drench.e: From Middle English drench, drenche (“beverage, drink; cup of drink, specifically a poisoned drink; medicinal potion, specifically an emetic (?)”), from Old English drenċ (“drink; draft, potion; dose (of medicine, poison, etc.)”), from Proto-West Germanic *dranki, from Proto-Germanic *drankiz (“drink; potion.
drench.g: A dose or draught of liquid medicine (especially one causing sleepiness) taken by a person; specifically, a (large) dose, or one forced or p

dress.e: Further akin to Latin regō. Russian наряжа́ть (narjažátʹ), наря́д (narjád) (akin to ряд (rjad), поря́док (porjádok)).
dress.g: To put clothes (or, formerly, armour) on (oneself or someone, a doll, a mannequin, etc.); to clothe.

dresser.e: From Middle English dressure, dressor, dressour, a borrowing from Old French drecëur, drecëure, from the verb dresser.
dresser.g: An item of kitchen furniture, like a cabinet with shelves, for storing crockery or utensils.

dresser.e: From Middle English dresser, equivalent to dress + -er.
dresser.g: One who dresses in a particular way.

drift.e: From Middle English drift, dryft (“act of driving, drove, shower of rain or snow, impulse”), from Old English *drift (“drift”), from Proto-Germanic *driftiz (“drift”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”). Equivalent to drive + -t.
drift.g: Movement; that which moves or is moved.

drink.e: From Middle English drynken, drinken, from Old English drincan (“to drink, swallow up, engulf”), from Proto-West Germanic *drinkan, from Proto-Germanic *drinkaną (“to drink”), of uncertain origin; possibly from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrenǵ- (“to draw into one's mouth, sip, gulp”), nasalised variant of *dʰreǵ- (“to draw, glide”).
drink.g: To consume (a liquid) through the mouth.

drink.e: From Middle English drink, drinke (also as drinche, drunch), from Old English drynċ, from Proto-Germanic *drunkiz, *drankiz.

drinker.e: From Middle English drinkere, drynkere, from Old English drincere (“drinker”), from Proto-Germanic *drinkārijaz (“drinker”), equivalent to drink + -er.

drinking.e: From Middle English. By surface analysis, drink + -ing.
drinking.g: An act or session by which drink is consumed, especially alcoholic beverages.

drip.e: From Middle English drippen, druppen, from Old English drypan, from Proto-Germanic *drupjaną (“to fall in drops, drip”), from Proto-Germanic *drupô (“drop”).
drip.g: To fall one drop at a time.

drip.e: From Middle English drippe, from the verb (see above).

drive.e: From Middle English dryven, from Old English drīfan (“to drive, force, move”), from Proto-West Germanic *drīban, from Proto-Germanic *drībaną (“to drive”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰreybʰ- (“to drive, push”).

driver.e: From Middle English drivere, dryvere, dryvare, equivalent to drive + -er.

driving.e: From Middle English dryvyng, drivende, from Old English drīfende, from Proto-Germanic *drībandz, present participle of Proto-Germanic *drībaną (“to drive”), equivalent to drive + -ing.

dromedary.e: From Middle English dromedari, dromedarie (“dromedary; any camel”), from Old French dromedaire, from Late Latin dromedārius (“kind of camel”), from Latin *dromadārius, from dromas, dromadis (“dromedary”) + -ārius (suffix forming nouns denoting agents of use). Dromas and dromadis are derived from Ancient Greek δρομᾰ́ς (dromắs, “running.

drop.e: From Late Middle English droppe, Middle English drope (“small quantity of liquid; small or least amount of something; pendant jewel; dripping of a liquid; a shower; nasal flow, catarrh; speck, spot; blemish; disease causing spots on the skin”), from Old English dropa (“a drop”), from Proto-West Germanic *dropō (“drop (of liquid)”).
drop.g: A small quantity of liquid, just large enough to hold its own rounded shape through surface tension, especially one that falls from a source

drop.e: From Middle English droppen, dropen (“to fall in drops, drip or trickle down; to scatter, sprinkle; to be covered with a liquid; to give off moisture; of an object: to drop, fall; of a living being: to fall to the ground”), from Old English droppian, dropian (“to drop”), from Proto-West Germanic *dropōn.
drop.g: Of a liquid: to fall in drops or droplets.

dropsy.e: From Middle English dropesie, idropesie, from Old French idropsie, ydropisie, from Latin hydrōps, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”).

dross.e: From Middle English drosse, dros, from Old English drōs, from Proto-Germanic *drōhs (“dregs, sediment”). Alternatively, this may be from *dragjō + *-snō (“yeast, sediment”; compare *dragjō (“yeast”)), as if from *drēcg + -sn. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dʰrā́ks (“sediment, yeast”). Related also to drast, dregs.

drought.e: From Middle English droughte, droghte, drouȝte, from Old English drūgaþ. By surface analysis, dry + -t (abstract nominal suffix).
drought.g: A period of unusually low rainfall, longer and more severe than a dry spell.

drove.e: From earlier drave, from Middle English drave, draf, from Old English drāf, first and third person singular indicative preterite of drīfan (“to drive”).
drove.g: To herd cattle; particularly over a long distance.

drown.e: From Middle English drownen, drounen, drunen (“to drown”), of obscure and uncertain origin. The OED suggests an unattested Old English form *drūnian. Harper 2001 points to Old English druncnian, ġedruncnian (> Middle English drunknen, dronknen (“to drown”)), "probably influenced" by Old Norse drukkna (cf. Icelandic drukkna, Danish drukne (“to drown”)).
drown.g: To die from suffocation while immersed in water or other fluid.

drowsy.e: From drowse + -y, despite the fact that drowsy (1520) is recorded before drowse (1570).
drowsy.g: Inclined to drowse; heavy with sleepiness

drunk.e: From Middle English drunke, drunken, ydrunke, ydrunken, from Old English druncen, ġedruncen (“drunk”), from Proto-Germanic *drunkanaz, *gadrunkanaz (“drunk; drunken”), past participle of Proto-Germanic *drinkaną (“to drink”).
drunk.g: Intoxicated as a result of excessive alcohol consumption, usually by drinking alcoholic beverages.

drunkard.e: From earlier droncarde, from Middle English *druncard (attested as a surname, Druncard), possibly from Middle Low German drunkert, equivalent to drunk + -ard (“pejorative agent suffix”).
drunkard.g: A person who is habitually drunk.

drunken.e: From Middle English drunken, ydronken, idrunken, from Old English druncen, ġedruncen (“drunk; drunken”), from Proto-Germanic *drunkanaz (“drunken”), past participle of Proto-Germanic *drinkaną (“to drink”), equivalent to drink + -en.
drunken.g: Drunk, in the state of intoxication after having drunk an alcoholic beverage.

dry.e: Adjective and noun from Middle English drye, dryge, drüȝe, from Old English drȳġe (“dry; parched, withered”), from Proto-West Germanic *drūgī, *draugī, from Proto-Germanic *drūgiz, *draugiz (“dry, hard”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰerǵʰ- (“to strengthen; become hard”), from *dʰer- (“to hold, support”). The verb derives from Middle English drien.
